stories.headline: Reflection ships Beam: a 501B-parameter open-weight MoE with 23B active, built for coding agents
stories.why_read: AI Top Story: Anand RT’d the launch and it’s #2 on HN (~474 points / 149 comments). An American open-weight model that sells on inference efficiency, with weights promised this month.
body: Reflection calls Beam its first open-weight model: a sparse Mixture-of-Experts with 501 billion total parameters and 23 billion active, aimed at coding, reasoning and agentic work. The blog says it was pretrained on 23.8 trillion tokens, and that the RL run generated more than 100 million rollouts on 10.5K NVIDIA GB300 GPUs over four weeks. Beam is still in final red-teaming. Early access is by sign-up, and weights, a technical report and a model card are due “later this month.”

The pitch is intelligence per token, not top scores. Reflection’s own table has Beam at 80.9 on SWE-bench Verified and 80.1 on Terminal Bench v2.1. It concedes Kimi K3 is ahead on raw capability, and claims reasoning scores comparable to GLM-5.2 at 3–4× less inference compute. Monday’s Diff had the pre-launch X News chatter. These are the actual numbers, though they are vendor benchmarks until the weights land and others can test them.

stories.headline: Nobel Prize in Physics 2026 goes to Francis Halzen for IceCube, the neutrino telescope buried in South Pole ice
stories.why_read: Non-AI Top Story: #1 on HN this morning. A cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice, wired with light sensors, opened a new kind of astronomy, and that is squarely the physics side of Anand’s pinned post.
body: The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the 2026 physics prize on 6 October to Francis Halzen of the University of Wisconsin–Madison, “for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin.” Halzen first proposed catching neutrinos in South Pole ice in 1988. IceCube now instruments an entire cubic kilometre of glacial ice and was finished in 2011. When a neutrino very occasionally hits an atomic nucleus, the flash of light is recorded by sensors in the clear ice.

Neutrinos are worth that effort because they arrive without bending or losing energy, so they point back to the cosmic particle accelerators that make them. Those sources fire particles up to a million times more energetic than anything built on Earth. Committee chair Mark Pearce credited Halzen’s “tenacity and scientific vision” with paving the way “for a new kind of astronomy.” This is a big-instrument, decades-long engineering win, and it follows Monday’s medicine prize for optogenetics.

stories.headline: A team of Claude Opus 5.5 agents proposes two room-temperature magnetic semiconductors for future memory
stories.why_read: Featured: HN ~372 / 252 comments. AI agents ran the DFT simulations and surfaced a 1999 compound hiding in plain sight, and the post ships its code and caveats.
body: Vals AI’s Geby Jaff writes that a team of Claude Opus 5.5 agents searched for “Luttinger-compensated” magnets: materials with zero net magnetism, like antiferromagnets, that still sort electrons by spin, which is what spintronic memory needs. The agents ran density functional theory at two levels (PBE+U and the slower HSE06). One candidate is a newly designed oxide, YBaMnFeO₅, predicted to have a 2.35 eV band gap and to stay magnetic to roughly 420–490 K. Its catch: the Mn/Fe checkerboard it needs falls apart around 950 K, below typical synthesis temperatures.

The more interesting find is KV[Cr(CN)₆], a Prussian-blue relative first made in 1999. A 2008 paper had already plotted its spin-sorted band edges without anyone calling it out. The agents predict a ~2.1 eV gap, and the 1999 sample stayed ordered to 376 K. The post is candid that the only sample is a wet powder and that the two simulation methods disagree on how much the water hurts. This is AI-for-science as a hypothesis generator with receipts, not yet a measured result.

stories.headline: SemiAnalysis limit-tests every AI subscription: Anthropic plans deliver 5x+ the value of OpenAI’s
stories.why_read: Featured: Anand RT’d it. A $200 plan isn’t worth a fixed amount; it depends on the plan, the model and the workload, and SemiAnalysis measured the meters.
body: SemiAnalysis (Andrew Megalaa, Max Kan and Dylan Patel) ran isolated experiments on Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, SpaceXAI, MiniMax, Moonshot, Z.ai, Cursor and Cognition plans. Each test pushes one token type (input, cache write, cache read or output) and watches how far the 5-hour and 7-day usage meters move. Their thesis is that a plan’s worth only makes sense as a (plan, model, workload) tuple, because credit costs can differ sharply from API price ratios. Labs can also change limits silently by retuning those credit costs.

The economics matter beyond hobbyists. By their rough Anthropic model, subscriptions are about 10% of revenue but can take more than 40% of inference compute. The piece also notes OpenAI cut its $200 plan’s usage in half and dropped relative-usage claims from its pricing page. It pairs with Monday’s Theo argument that Anthropic’s code models pulled ahead. The headline is from the free part; the detailed dashboard is paywalled.

stories.headline: mold 3.0: the fastest Linux linker is now written in Rust, with zero regressions across all of Gentoo
stories.why_read: Featured: Anand RT’d it. A drop-in C++→Rust rewrite of core build infrastructure, held to a strict bar and shipped.
body: Rui Ueyama’s mold 3.0.0 release notes say the C++ codebase has been rewritten in Rust and that 2.42.1 was the last C++ release. 3.0 is meant as a drop-in replacement: same command-line options, same target architectures, same output apart from listed bug fixes, and linking performance on par. The team checked this by running the test suite on every supported target, comparing output across real-world workloads, and building all Gentoo packages, with no regressions found.

The safety win is concrete. Corrupted input that could make the C++ version read out of bounds and segfault now hits a bounds check and panics cleanly. CMake is gone in favour of Cargo (Rust 1.95+), and the goal for 3.x is GNU ld linker-script compatibility so distros can make mold the default. For someone who has run enterprise build platforms, this is a rare example of rewriting a hot path in a new language without the users having to notice.

stories.headline: A Cybertruck on FSD crosses three lanes from a red light to clear a path for an ambulance
stories.why_read: Featured: Anand RT’d the video. It’s a deliberate yield from a full stop, not a simple pull-over, and X News picked it up as a showcase.
body: @mrtimer2022: “I’m at a red light in the middle of 5 lanes of traffic. My Cybertruck sees an ambulance approaching from the rear… but the intersection is mostly blocked. So, it turns right across 3 lanes into a safe pocket, leaving a clear lane for the emergency vehicle to proceed without pause.” The truck then merged back and “automatically updat[ed] my nav to reflect the unplanned turn.” The poster’s point: “this wasn’t just a pull over while driving.”

X News framed it as a highlight of FSD behaviour, alongside the usual counter-clips and the camera-only versus multi-sensor argument. A separate X News item spotlighted an owner whose app shows 98.1% of 26,282 miles driven on FSD. These are anecdotes and fan-shared dashboards, not fleet statistics, but emergency-vehicle handling is the kind of edge case the robotaxi debate turns on.

stories.headline: A Florida woman used Claude as a diary; Anthropic flagged a threat to police and she now faces a felony
stories.why_read: Featured: the day’s biggest HN thread (~744 points / 575 comments). A real-world line where AI safety review meets privacy.
body: TechSpot reports that Carli Michelle Heller of Bonita Springs wrote to Claude on September 26 that she would “shoot up” the Sheriff’s office, and later said she uses the chatbot like a “diary.” Claude’s safety systems flagged the entry, a human reviewer judged it a credible threat, and Anthropic reported it to law enforcement. Anthropic says it may share user information in limited emergencies to prevent death or serious injury. Deputies detained her without incident, and she is charged under Florida Statute 836.10, a second-degree felony for written threats.

The backdrop is the pressure running the other way: TechSpot notes British Columbia is suing OpenAI and Sam Altman over a mass shooting by someone OpenAI had flagged but never referred to police. The takeaway for anyone running agents against their own data is plain. A chatbot conversation is not a private notebook, and providers will escalate what their systems judge to be credible threats.

stories.headline: TSMC hits a record after Musk confirms early talks on Terafab, his Texas chip-fab project
stories.why_read: Featured: X News. A possible TSMC-run fab serving Tesla, SpaceX and SpaceXAI in Texas, with nothing signed yet.
body: X News reports that TSMC’s U.S.-listed shares rose 2.7% Monday to close at $485.80, pushing its market value past $2.5 trillion, after Elon Musk replied to a report about possible collaboration on Terafab, his chip project in Texas. The talks could see TSMC operate a new fab serving Tesla, SpaceX and SpaceXAI as AI and robotics demand climbs. Intel fell more than 3%, possibly on the added competition.

Nothing is final, and the summary stresses that any structure is preliminary. For a Texan who tracks the Musk companies and the chip supply chain, though, it ties together this week’s threads: SpaceX’s 10 GW compute buildout, the GPU scramble, and the idea that the Musk ecosystem wants its own leading-edge capacity rather than waiting in Nvidia’s line.

stories.headline: Wall Street assembles a $60B debt package to finance Anthropic’s Broadcom-supplied TPU lease
stories.why_read: X News: the largest AI-hardware financing yet, built on a “sell-lend-own” vehicle around a $125.2B five-year chip lease.
body: X News says Bank of America, Citi and Morgan Stanley lead a record package: $42 billion of senior debt backed by Broadcom’s credit and $18 billion of junior debt, including a $9 billion commitment from Blackstone. The money supports Anthropic’s $125.2 billion five-year lease of Google-designed TPUs supplied by Broadcom. A special vehicle buys the chips and leases them to Anthropic.

It follows a $35 billion deal in June as Anthropic eyes an IPO, and it tests how much AI debt credit markets will absorb given chip depreciation risk. Read it next to the SemiAnalysis subscription piece: the generous plans run on compute financed like infrastructure.

stories.headline: SpaceX’s 10 GW of AI compute: reportedly 60% for its own use, and a pitch for a new data center every month
stories.why_read: Anand bookmarked both: Jukan on the internal/external split and NextBigFuture on build speed as the real SpaceX AI story.
body: @jukan05: “Apparently 60% of $SPCX’s 10GW goes to its own demand, and only 40% is for external customers. Could it be because Grok Bot has been a hit?” That is an unconfirmed “apparently,” but it fits the Grok Bot adoption stories in Anand’s feed.

@nextbigfuture’s Brian Wang argues Wall Street still underrates construction speed: SpaceX AI data centers going up in about five months versus two to four years elsewhere, “roughly a 5–10X difference,” with overlapping projects heading toward a new completion every month. His video covers Macrohard, Macroharder and Minihard, the effect of power, cooling and chip supply, GB300 and Rubin per-site compute, and valuation scenarios behind a $652/share figure. Treat it as an enthusiast’s model, not guidance.

stories.headline: Austin robotaxi edge cases: a Cybercab loops a parking lot for 14 minutes, while traffic cams count more Teslas than Waymos
stories.why_read: X News: one honest failure and one bullish snapshot from Anand’s own city, both worth reading with a grain of salt.
body: X News says autonomous-driving tester David Moss watched his Cybercab circle a Bassett Home Furnishings lot in Austin for 14 minutes because construction blocked the exit. The car never rerouted or got a remote operator, and the arrival time on screen never arrived. Support eventually restarted FSD remotely and the crew moved its truck. It echoes an earlier hotel-lot loop. The car stayed safe, but it shows dynamic-obstacle navigation is still a gap.

Separately, Steven Spencer shared Austin traffic-cam snapshots showing Tesla robotaxis edging out Waymo sightings over one 24-hour window. Farzad hailed it as a milestone, while others pointed to heavy rain sidelining some Waymos and to Waymo’s much larger national footprint. Taken together with Monday’s “Cybercabs are everywhere” post, these are the real street-level texture of the ramp.

stories.headline: Gas-powered cars fall below 50% of global new-vehicle sales for the first time
stories.why_read: Anand RT’d it: 49%, down from 73% in 2021, though the U.S. is moving the other way after incentives ended.
body: @GuyDealership: “Gas-powered cars are now under 50% of global new-vehicle sales: First time ever. Share sits at 49%, down from 73% in 2021, according to Mobility Global Data.” The post adds that in the U.S. “we’re seeing a slightly different situation, with gas cars regaining some traction after federal incentives went away.”

This is a single-source stat from a dealer-industry account, so check how hybrids are counted before quoting it. Still, it’s an energy-transition milestone that fits the Energy Technology part of Anand’s pinned post.

stories.headline: John Arnold’s list of how the energy industry consolidated in Houston since 2000
stories.why_read: Anand bookmarked it: a Texas-sized map of headquarters moves from Dallas, Oklahoma, California, Colorado and beyond.
body: @johnarnold: “It’s not just OKC. Since 2000, there’s been a massive consolidation of the energy industry to Houston.” His “highly incomplete list” includes moves from Dallas (Halliburton, Exxon, XTO, Pioneer), California (Oxy, Chevron, Calpine), Oklahoma (Citgo, Devon, Phillips Petroleum), Louisiana (McDermott, Tidewater), Colorado (Cimarex, Whiting, PDC), the Northeast (Schlumberger US, NRG, Talen) and Canada (Enbridge US).
For an Austin resident watching Texas pull in AI fabs, robotaxis and data centers, it’s a reminder that the state’s earlier energy cluster formed through the same kind of slow gravitational pull.

stories.headline: Grok Bot’s newer features in practice: main bot, team bots, inline mini apps, and voice that does real tasks
stories.why_read: Anand RT’d Riley Brown’s walkthrough; X News collects users praising voice mode for actual work.
body: @rileybrown: “GrokBot recently dropped 4 new features that I found incredibly useful in my business... and not enough people are talking about them.” His chaptered video covers the Primary/Main Bot, Team Bot, Inline Mini Apps for Slack and Gmail, and “Bypass Bot Blockers,” plus a bonus tip.

X News separately says users like @poteto are praising Grok Bot’s voice mode on desktop and mobile for real work such as invoice processing and supplier follow-ups. Anand runs a named Grok Bot fleet, so this is practical notes from other operators of the same setup. Expect some promotional gloss.

stories.headline: What people actually use to manage coding agents, and the case for skipping specs and tickets
stories.why_read: Anand RT’d three takes: a crowd-sourced “Linear for agents” list, a no-spec workflow, and HumanLayer’s outline skill.
body: @aishwarya_08 asked whether there is a “Linear for agents” and summarized 100+ replies: Linear itself via its MCP, @herdrdev (“repeatedly called the most polished way to manage multiple agents”), @orca_build, @t3dotcodes for sessions across remote machines, Nous Research’s Hermes Agent for its kanban board, and plain GitHub issues plus the gh CLI. Her warning: “about 30+ people are building this exact product right now, so choose wisely!”

@rockatanescu argues that since Sol 5.6/Opus 5, writing a spec and splitting it into tickets is the wrong approach: “Just tell the agent what you want to do and it will do it,” and for large tasks, discuss with the agent how to split the work into several shippable PRs. @dexhorthy compared a new planning tool to the “outline” skill HumanLayer bundles, which mixes /show-me with a planning language.

stories.headline: “The abstraction was the overhead”: from LangChain to hand-rolled agent loops and markdown “skills”
stories.why_read: Anand bookmarked Arpit Bhayani and RT’d Markus Eisele: two sharp one-liners on how agent engineering got simpler and odder.
body: @arpit_bhayani: “we all rushed in 2023-24 to learn LangChain and many other frameworks. And now, almost all major coding harnesses and agents are just hand-rolled loops. Turns out, the abstraction was the overhead.” @myfear, in the same vein: “I still can’t wrap my head around the fact that people get famous for writing markdown files, calling them engineering skills and putting them on GitHub.”

Anand also bookmarked @TurnerNovak quoting Marc Andreessen on 20VC: “You have to be a frontier model, you have to upgrade yourself every few weeks.” Read together, the advice is to keep the stack thin and keep your own skills current.

stories.headline: Atlassian publishes its AI-native SDLC playbook: the bottleneck moves to planning, review and maintenance
stories.why_read: Anand RT’d it, and it lands squarely on his day job: enterprise DevOps for 30k+ engineers in the agent era.
body: Atlassian’s “AI SDLC transformation playbook” argues that AI-native development goes far beyond handing developers coding agents. As coding becomes “asynchronous, multi-threaded,” the steps before and after code (planning, design, review, maintenance) become the biggest bottlenecks, and so does team collaboration. It frames seven pillars: platform investments in context (a “context graph”) and measurement, plus workflow shifts across each SDLC phase.

Matthew Canham’s announcement says it is informed by Atlassian’s own transformation and by top engineering orgs it works with, with print copies at Team ’26 EU this week. It’s vendor content, but the frame of a “modern software factory” that is event-driven and reshaped around human judgment is the conversation enterprise platform teams are having right now.

stories.headline: Mitchell Hashimoto’s Superlogical opens public testing of Rex, a free self-hostable terminal with persistent sessions
stories.why_read: Anand RT’d it: the Ghostty creator’s next act is a drop-in terminal with remote servers and no account required.
body: Superlogical says Rex is “a drop-in replacement for whichever terminal you use today,” with persistent sessions, responsive remote connections and program activity status. Testing starts with the macOS app, which self-hosts its own Rex server and can connect to others. Linux and Windows servers and iOS, Linux and Windows clients exist “at varying stages of readiness.” About 50 private testers have used it for real work for months.

The terms are notable: “Rex is and will always be free,” no account needed, fully self-hostable, and “we do not see or share your data.” A commercialization plan is promised before stable release. For a terminal-first engineer since IRIX, this is worth joining the mailing-list queue for. Invites go out in signup order.

stories.headline: Obsidian 1.14: edit Markdown outside your vault, Quick Look previews, iOS Quick Capture, and Kanban in Bases
stories.why_read: Anand RT’d it. His bots file notes into a Dropbox Obsidian vault, so these features touch his daily workflow.
body: @obsdmd lists five major improvements in Obsidian 1.14: “1. Edit Markdown files outside your vault 2. Preview files using macOS Quick Look when the app is closed 3. Instantly add notes with Quick Capture on iOS 4. Kanban and new grouping options in Bases 5. Highlight colors.”

Editing files outside the vault and Kanban views in Bases matter most for a setup where agents write Markdown into weekly folders: one opens up files that live elsewhere, the other turns structured notes into a board without plugins.

stories.headline: DHH on the Rust speed debate: “Programming tribalism is a hell of a drug”
stories.why_read: Anand bookmarked DHH and RT’d a post asking why we fight over languages. It lands nicely next to mold’s Rust rewrite.
body: @dhh: “I can’t believe that we’re actually debating whether or why Rust — a systems level language meant to rival C/C++!! — would be much faster than the interpreted or GC-using alternatives people have historically used for web apps. Programming tribalism is a hell of a drug!”

Anand also RT’d @AstraKernel, who asked ChatGPT why humans fight to prove their choices are best. The same day, mold shipped a Rust rewrite whose release bar was the same options, the same output, the same speed and no regressions, which is more useful than any argument about languages.

stories.headline: Dust: pretraining transformers without backpropagation, competitive with backprop at large populations
stories.why_read: HN ~211 points: a zeroth-order method that gets more population-efficient as models grow, a bitter-lesson bet against backprop.
body: Q Labs presents Dust as the first zeroth-order method competitive with backprop at pretraining transformer language models. It perturbs activations independently at every token, so each token acts as a virtual population member and one forward pass evaluates them all. At large population sizes, which means substantially more compute, it closely approximates backprop and “in multiple settings even exceeds it.” By the authors’ extrapolation it is 10³–10⁴× more efficient than a transformer version of the EGGROLL evolution-strategies method.

The surprising result is the scaling direction: larger models were more population-efficient, with a 243M-parameter model beating one 120× smaller at most population sizes, and gradient alignment held up to 1B tokens. It’s early, small-scale research, but it is a serious attempt at search-based learning that could free architectures from needing to be differentiable.

stories.headline: ChatGPT is forging real New Yorker cartoonists’ signatures on AI-made cartoons
stories.why_read: HN ~461 / 338 comments: Nieman Lab documents more than 15 cartoonists whose signatures ChatGPT reproduced.
body: Nieman Lab’s Andrew Deck traces a viral ChatGPT cartoon of Dolly Parton and Tim Curry at the pearly gates, signed “BLOPER,” the pen name of New Yorker cartoonist Brendan Loper, who never drew it. “My name is my name. It felt very much like a violation of my personhood,” Loper said. Deck found more than 15 New Yorker cartoonists whose signatures OpenAI’s image generator used without permission, including Harry Bliss, Emily Flake and Joe Dator.

OpenAI thanked the community for “flagging bugs and unintended behavior,” and ChatGPT began warning that such prompts “may violate our guardrails,” but it still signed some generic cartoons at publication. A New Yorker spokesperson said Condé Nast never granted an LLM developer permission to train on its cartoons. Signatures function as provenance watermarks, which is why this matters.

stories.headline: GNOME’s Michael Catanzaro: there’s “zero hope” of quality software in 2026 without AI vulnerability scanning
stories.why_read: HN: a GNOME developer reverses his own stance, saying AI bug reports are no longer slop and projects that ban them should leave GNOME.
body: Catanzaro opens by quoting his own GUADEC talk abstracts about how impossible it is to write secure C, C++ or Vala, then says the landscape changed completely in a year. “There is zero hope of maintaining quality software in 2026 without AI vulnerability scanning,” he writes, pointing to the “tremendous quantity of bugs” found in GLib and fwupd, and to AI making working exploits easier to build. He notes Daniel Stenberg sees the same improvement in report quality for curl.

He doesn’t hide the costs: reports that are verbose, exaggerate severity, or occasionally contain fabricated stack traces, and volume that overwhelms volunteers. His proposal is still blunt: GNOME projects should permit AI-generated vulnerability reports, and ones that keep banning them “are no longer suitable dependencies for GNOME.” It is directly relevant to any enterprise secure-DevOps program.

stories.headline: ASOS app users get an extortion push notification: “we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance”
stories.why_read: HN, via the BBC: attackers apparently turned a retailer’s own app into a ransom note, a breach that suggests more than one credential.
body: BBC cyber correspondent Joe Tidy reports that ASOS users across the UK received a pop-up from the app reading: “Dear ASOS DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it.” ASOS did not immediately respond. It is not known whether ASOS uses Snowflake or what data, if any, sits there. Snowflake environments have featured in breaches tied to Ticketmaster and Santander.

Horizon3’s Dan Bird points out that sending pushes requires access to the notification system, which is separate from any data warehouse. If both claims hold, “the attackers got hold of credentials that opened more than one door.” The lesson for platform teams: push-notification keys are production credentials and need the same scoping and rotation as everything else.

stories.headline: A known ballot-scanner shuffle flaw let a non-expert with AI tools reorder 1.5M Georgia primary ballots
stories.why_read: HN: Princeton CITP shows how an unpatched 2022 vulnerability plus public records can strip ballot secrecy.
body: Max Springer, writing for Princeton’s Center for Information Technology Policy, says ballot scanners in several states shuffle electronic records before release to keep them anonymous, but a vulnerability disclosed in 2022 lets the shuffle be reversed, and some states haven’t applied the fix. “I am not a security researcher,” he writes, yet within a few hours, using AI tools and only public records, he reconstructed the order of 1.5 million ballots in Georgia’s May 2026 primary, 98.9% of in-person ballots.

Combine that order with the state’s public logs of when people voted, and in some counties every vote-center ballot can be tied to its voter. The post is from August but surfaced on HN today. It is a clear case of AI lowering the skill floor for an old, unpatched bug, which is the same point Catanzaro makes from the defender’s side.

stories.headline: Alman and Vassilevska Williams claim truly subquadratic 3SUM and subcubic APSP, refuting two core hardness hypotheses
stories.why_read: HN: if it holds up, this is a landmark in fine-grained complexity, the mathematics corner of Anand’s pinned post.
body: A new arXiv paper by Josh Alman and Virginia Vassilevska Williams claims the first polynomial improvements over textbook algorithms: deterministic 3SUM on n polynomial-size integers in O(n^1.9992) time, and APSP on directed n-vertex graphs with polynomially bounded integer weights in O(n^2.9995). The abstract says this refutes the 3SUM and APSP hypotheses, and through known reductions also the Exact Triangle and Zero-Weight k-Clique hypotheses, among others.

Everything follows from one new algorithm for thin matrix products, built by modifying a variant of Coppersmith’s rectangular matrix multiplication. The exponents are tiny improvements, but many conditional lower bounds in algorithms rest on these hypotheses, so a lot of “provably optimal” results would need rethinking. It is a fresh preprint, so expect scrutiny.

stories.headline: Med-El’s TICI Unico, the first fully implanted cochlear implant, reaches its first patients
stories.why_read: HN, via IEEE Spectrum: microphone, processor and battery all under the scalp, so users can hear while asleep or swimming.
body: IEEE Spectrum’s Edd Gent reports that Austrian company Med-El has launched the TICI Unico, the first commercially available totally implantable cochlear implant, after more than 15 years of development. It has European approval but is not yet available in the U.S., and the first four commercial implantations happened the morning of the announcement. A 30-patient trial found hearing “comparable” to Med-El’s conventional implants.

“For the first time, all components of a cochlear implant, including the microphone, are implanted beneath the skin,” said CEO Ingeborg Hochmair, who helped develop one of the first multichannel implants in the 1970s. Users can hear while sleeping, swimming and recharging. It’s a hardware story with a direct human payoff.

stories.headline: Gleam v1.19 stops emitting Erlang source and generates Erlang abstract forms directly
stories.why_read: HN: faster builds, exact line numbers in BEAM stack traces, and the end of “transpiler” as an insult.
body: Louis Pilfold writes that Giacomo Cavalieri rewrote Gleam’s Erlang code generator to output Erlang abstract forms, the intermediate tree the Erlang compiler normally builds from source, in its binary external term format. That lets Gleam load generated code directly and skip the front half of the Erlang compiler.

The payoff: significantly shorter build times on Erlang (benchmarked with a variant of José Valim’s langcompilebench), runtime location metadata that matches the original Gleam source so crash reports and stack traces are exact, and a potential path to debugger support. Pilfold’s aside: “We never have to hear someone use the word ‘transpiler’ as a pejorative ever again.”

stories.headline: “Friendship ended with Deno, now Node is my best friend”: a long-time Deno user moves back to Node
stories.why_read: HN ~194 / 112 comments: Node v26 got good enough that a site migration was mostly import swaps, and builds came out 15% faster.
body: David Bushell says a month of heavy Node work on a SvelteKit project made him ask “When did Node get so good‽” He paired Node with FNM and PNPM (aliasing npm to pnpm), set pnpm-workspace.yaml to a one-day minimumReleaseAge and a no-downgrade trust policy to avoid the next Shai-Hulud-style supply-chain hit, and notes PNPM blocks post-install scripts. His complaint is that Node strips TypeScript types but refuses to inside node_modules.

Migrating his static site generator on Node v26.10.0 meant swapping Deno’s file system API for node:fs and Deno.serve for Hono’s Node adapter, and builds came out 15% faster. His blunt verdict on Deno, the company: it “stopped innovating” years ago. It’s a practitioner’s view of supply-chain hygiene as much as a runtime review.

stories.headline: Example.com gets its biggest redesign in decades: six languages, a character-by-character fade, and a bandwidth rationale
stories.why_read: HN ~241 / 157 comments: a fun bit of internet history, plus IANA explaining why the page changed.
body: DebugBear notes that until 28 September 2026 example.com was a static English page. The redesign uses JavaScript to rotate its explanation every five seconds through English, Arabic, Chinese, French, Russian and Spanish, adds an SVG book icon, and fades each character in its own span with staggered transition delays. The new message warns: “This is not a service, avoid relying on it for testing and monitoring purposes.”

IANA’s statement explains that the domain is heavily trafficked and mostly by automated clients, so the page was split into a minimal HTML document plus a separate JavaScript file that bots tend not to fetch, cutting bandwidth. The post then walks through versions back to a 2002 table layout with the ICANN logo. Anyone who has hard-coded example.com into a health check should take the hint.
